reader.title: Threatened lynching of the McVeigh murder suspects at Muskogee
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: The only report of the episode says a lynching of two prisoners held at Muskogee was prevented by a heavy guard, so it is a threatened lynching; the threatened men were described as Indians, not Black (A7).
No one was killed: the Bazoo says a lynching was prevented by a heavy guard, and it describes no mob, its size, or its stated motive (A7).
The threatened lynching rests on one second-hand report in the Sedalia Bazoo (A7); the wire briefs corroborate only the underlying Eufaula killing (A1, A4, A5).

summary.text: The threatened lynching of the McVeigh murder suspects at Muskogee was a prevented mob killing of two prisoners, described as Indians, held at Muskogee, Indian Territory, in late December 1880 for the killing of Elias McVeigh near Eufaula.
According to the Sedalia Weekly Bazoo, a heavy guard was needed to prevent the lynching, and the prisoners were to be taken in shackles to Ft. Smith, Arkansas.
The threat is known from that single second-hand report, while the killing itself ran widely as a St. Louis wire item.
A St. Louis dispatch of December 16 said that two "full-blooded Indians" went to the house of Elias McVeigh in Eufala on Tuesday, accepted his hospitality, and then shot and killed him.
The same dispatch said they wounded a hired man named Barret or Barrett with an ax, "inflicting mortal wounds."
A ready-print brief dated the killing to the 14th and added that "it is believed the Indians were hired to do the deed."
The German-language Westbote gave more detail, placing McVeigh's property six miles from Eufaula and saying he was shot from behind while tending a sick child.
It also reported that a white Eufaula resident whom McVeigh had sued for theft was said to have hired the killers.
On January 3, 1881, an unnamed man who came in "from the Nation" told a Bazoo reporter that the two Indians accused of the killing were still held at Muskogee.
He said that "it was with considerable difficulty a lynching was prevented, a heavy guard being required for that purpose."
The report does not say who sought to lynch the prisoners, how many there were, or when the attempt was made.
The authorities intended to move the prisoners to Ft. Smith on January 4, shackled together with a "negro burglar" held for robbing a Muskogee store on Christmas day.
The burglar was not accused in the Eufaula killing, and the report does not say he was threatened.
No report of the prisoners' arrival at Ft. Smith, an indictment, or a trial appears in the coverage.
The killing reached papers from Sacramento and Cheyenne to St. Paul on December 17 as a St. Louis wire brief, under heads such as "Indian Deviltry" and "A Brutal Crime."
Shorter ready-print versions ran in the Milan Exchange and the Iola Register a week later.
Only the Sedalia Weekly Bazoo, relying on a traveler's account, reported the prevented lynching, in one sentence under the headline "Two Murderers and a Burglar."
The episode predates the Black newspapers in the collection, and no Black-press account was found.
The papers differ on the hired man, whom the wire called Barret or Barrett and the Bazoo called McGuire.
The wire said he was given mortal wounds with an ax, the Bazoo that he was "mutilated," and the ready-print brief that he was murdered.

accounts.label: St. Louis wire report
accounts.gist: Two full-blooded Indians accepted McVeigh's hospitality at Eufala, then shot and killed him and cut his hired man with an ax; it says nothing of a lynching threat.

accounts.label: Ready-print and German-language briefs
accounts.gist: The Indians were believed to have been hired; Der Westbote said a white Eufaula resident whom McVeigh had sued for theft hired them.

accounts.label: Informant to the Sedalia Bazoo
accounts.gist: An unnamed gentleman from the Nation said a lynching of the two prisoners at Muskogee was prevented with difficulty by a heavy guard.

framing.detail: Papers ran the St. Louis brief on the killing under heads such as 'Indian Deviltry' and 'A Brutal Crime'.
The Bazoo reported the prevented lynching in a single sentence, without comment, and called the prisoners 'murderers' in its headline.

conflicts.note: The wire and ready-print briefs agree on Barrett; the Bazoo's 'McGuire' rests on a second-hand informant.

versions.value: crippled or chopped with an ax, 'inflicting mortal wounds'

conflicts.note: No report of his death beyond the ready-print brief was found.

record_check.record: Two Indiana men accused of murdering two white men
record_check.dossier: The accused were 'two Indians'; one man (McVeigh) was killed and his hired man wounded.

record_check.record: murdering white men McVey and Mutt and mutilating McClure at Eufaula
record_check.dossier: Accused of killing Elias McVeigh (McVey) and wounding his hired man Barrett (McGuire in the Bazoo); there is no 'Mutt' or 'McClure'.
December 14, 1880 is the date of the Eufaula killing; the lynching threat at Muskogee came later, at an unstated date before January 3, 1881.
The threatened men were described as Indians; the only Black person mentioned, a burglar, is not said to have been threatened.
Correct: the prisoners were in custody under a heavy guard.

info: The underlying killing at Eufaula took place on Tuesday the 14th of December 1880; the threatened lynching occurred while the prisoners were held at Muskogee, at an unstated date before January 3, 1881.
Muskogee, Indian Territory (where the prisoners were held); the killing was at or six miles from Eufaula, I. T.

The men threatened were two unnamed prisoners described as 'Indians' ('full-blooded Indians' in the wire report); a 'negro burglar' was held and shackled with them but is not said to have been threatened.
Accused of killing Elias McVeigh (McVey) and wounding his hired man, named McGuire (Bazoo) or Barret/Barrett (wire), with an ax at Eufaula.
Not described; the Bazoo says only that a lynching was prevented.
The prisoners were still held at Muskogee on January 3, 1881, and were to be shackled together with the burglar and taken to Ft. Smith the next day.
